Judgment:

1. This appeal under Section 378 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) lays challenge to the judgment dated 06.10.2023 passed by the Ld. CMM, Rouse Avenue District Court, New Delhi whereby both the respondents had been acquitted of the charge for the commission of the offence punishable under Section 120B IPC read with Sections 3 & 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955.

sentences.text:
The brief background relevant for the disposal of the appeal is as under:
2.1.

On 31.05.2011, CBI filed the chargesheet for the commission of the offence punishable under Section 120B IPC read with Section 3 & 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 against the respondents herein and one Smt. Sushila Rani,
who was the proprietor of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company.

2.2. By way of the Dealership Agreement dated 25.01.1990, M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company had been appointed as the dealer of M/s. Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (for short 'BPCL') in respect of the petroleum products namely Light CBI v.
Praveen Garg & Anr. Page No. 2 of 26 Diesel Oil and Superior Kerosene Oil.

Light CBI v.
Praveen Garg & Anr
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: As per the charge sheet, the firm was also the authorized dealer of Furnace Oil.

2.3. M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company was also having the Kerosene License No.
3614/19 dated 20.02.1990 issued by the Food and Supply Department, Govt. of NCT of Delhi to procure the kerosene oil from BPCL and supply it to the kerosene oil depots under the public distribution system.

As per the prevalent practice and the terms of license, no licensee was authorized to store/decant any quantity of kerosene oil meant for the kerosene oil depots at any place before its delivery and was required to submit the acknowledgment/compliance report of delivery to the concerned kerosene oil depots within 36 hours.

2.4. In nutshell, it was alleged in the charge-sheet that despite having the dealership of Light Diesel Oil and Superior Kerosene Oil only, Smt. Sushila Rani in conspiracy with the respondents used to store High Speed Diesel in contravention of Section 2 (f) read with Section 3 of the Motor Spirit and High Speed Diesel (Regulation of Supply, Distribution and Prevention of Malpractices) Order, 2005.

sentences.text: Apart from High Speed Diesel, they were also unauthorizedly storing kerosene oil and CBS Haldia.

Further, they used to bring blue colour kerosene oil of public CBI v. Praveen Garg & Anr. Page No. 3 of 26 distribution system meant for kerosene oil depots to the premises of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company and after decolouring it with the help of bleaching powder and other chemicals, used to mix the same with other standard petroleum products and sell the adulterated petroleum products to different companies and factories in contravention of Section 3 read with Section 4 of the Kerosene (Restriction on Use and Fixation of Ceiling Price) Order, 1993 and the Delhi Kerosene Oil (Export and Price) Control Order, 1962.
2.5.

Based on visual observation and density checking, Sh. K.G. Ghatwai, Senior Manager, Quality Control Cell, BPCL, who was a member of the team, informed that the petroleum products contained in all the four underground tanks and the Syntex tank appeared to be adulterated.
Thus, samples from the underground tanks as well as the Syntex tank were drawn and sealed in the presence of the independent witness Sh. Ashok Kumar Aggarwal.
Samples of Hydrogen Peroxide and unknown chemical found at the premises were also taken.

Out of three sets of samples of seven products,
one set of samples was given to Sh. K.G. Ghatwai and second set of samples was retained by the CBI Officers.
At the time of inspection, three employees of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company namely Sh. Virender Kumar, CBI v. Praveen Garg & Anr.
Page No. 5 of 26 Sh. Giriraj Kumar and Sh. Suraj were found present at the premises and they informed that they were working for Sh. Praveen Garg (the respondent no.1).
Since the respondent no.1 failed to join the surprise check, third set of samples was handed over to the representative/employee of the firm namely Sh. Giriraj.
Videography of the premises was also carried out by the technical team of CBI.
2.7. FIR bearing RC No. 0722010(E)0004/2010 was registered on 12.05.2010.
The respondent no.1 was arrested on 13.05.2010.

During his custodial interrogation, it transpired that in or around the year 2006, the respondent no.1 had taken over the business of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company from its proprietor Smt.
Sushila Rani on account of her old age and that he had got executed a General Power of Attorney dated 01.08.2006 in favour of his brother in law Sh. Mukesh Goel (respondent no.2) authorizing him to manage the business affairs of the firm for which the respondent no.1 used to pay an amount of Rs.15,000/- per month to Smt. Sushila Rani.
2.8.

During investigation, Smt. Sushila Rani maintained that though she is the proprietor of M/s.
Lakra Oil Trading Company but she had handed over the business affairs of the firm to both the CBI v. Praveen Garg & Anr. Page No. 6 of 26 respondents.
She also produced the attested photocopy of General Power of Attorney dated 01.08.2006 executed by her in favour of the respondent no.2.

However, investigation revealed that she was actively involved in the affairs of the firm along with the respondents and had also signed the inspection report dated 30.04.2010 conducted by the Cbi vs Sh.Praveen Garg And Anr on 6 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/95741817/

sentences.text: The samples of the products collected during the surprise check on 12.05.2010 were got analyzed from Quality Control Laboratory of BPCL.
Sample test reports dated 20.05.2010 confirmed adulteration as the samples failed to meet the standard specifications of the petroleum products.

The petroleum products seized were thus confiscated vide order dated 25.08.2010 of the Deputy Commissioner/Collector, East District, Delhi and pursuant to the said order, BPCL evacuated the entire confiscated petroleum products from the premises of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company between 15.10.2010 to 21.10.2010.
2.10.

On the basis of material produced with the chargesheet, cognizance of the offence punishable under Section 120B IPC read with Sections 3 & 7 of Essential Commodities Act was taken on 28.06.2011 and the respondents as well as Smt. Sushila CBI v. Praveen Garg & Anr. Page No. 7 of 26 Rani were summoned by the Ld. Trial Court.

sentences.text: Vide order 07.01.2013, charge for the commission of the abovesaid offence was directed to be framed against them.
Formal charge was framed on 11.01.2013.
However, Smt. Sushila Rani preferred Criminal Revision Petition No. 04/2013 against the order on charge before the Ld. Sessions Court.

Vide order dated 05.06.2013, the said revision petition was allowed and the Ld. Sessions Court discharged Smt. Sushila Rani by observing that after the execution of General Power of Attorney dated 01.08.2006, she had no concern with the day to day affairs of the firm.
Order dated 05.06.2013 was not challenged by the CBI and has attained finality.
2.11. During the course of trial, CBI examined 31 witnesses.
Statements of the respondents under Section 313 CrPC were recorded on 14.02.2023 wherein they denied the allegations against them and claimed innocence.
However, they chose not to lead evidence in their defence.

2.12. Vide the judgment dated 06.10.2023, the Ld. Trial Court acquitted both the respondents, by inter alia observing that since the prosecution had failed to prove the execution of General Power of Attorney dated 01.08.2006 by Smt. Sushila Rani in CBI v. Praveen Garg & Anr. Page No. 8 of 26 favour of the respondent no.2 Sh. Mukesh Goel, Smt. Sushila Rani alone was responsible for the affairs of the firm being the dealer and license holder of the petroleum products; and that no evidence had been produced to show the involvement of the respondents in unauthorized storage and adulteration of the petroleum products at the premises of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company.
Aggrieved therefrom, CBI has preferred the instant appeal before this Court.
3. Arguments advanced by the Senior PP for CBI and the counsel for both the respondents have been heard.
Trial court record has also been perused.

sentences.text: Senior PP for CBI has assailed the impugned judgment by contending that the Ld. Trial Court had failed to appreciate the evidence available on record.
He has submitted that PW-3 Sh. Suraj, who was the employee of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company, had categorically deposed that the respondent no. 2 Sh. Mukesh Goel was the owner of the said firm.

He has submitted that the customers of the said firm had also deposed that they used to deal with the respondents for purchase of CBI v. Praveen Garg & Anr. Page No. 9 of 26 furnace oil from the firm.

He has submitted that it is also the matter of record that the respondent no. 2 Sh. Mukesh Goel had got released the articles such as motor-pumps etc. on superdari in the capacity of authorized representative of the firm.

He has argued that the Ld. Trial Court failed to appreciate that the above material was sufficient to prove that the respondents were managing the affairs of the firm and thus, mere non-production of the original General Power of Attorney dated 01.08.2006 executed by Smt.
Sushila Rani in favour of Sh. Mukesh Goel (respondent no.2) could not have been deemed as fatal to the case of the prosecution.
5.

He has also submitted that during the surprise check conducted on 12.05.2010, huge quantities of unauthorized petroleum products including High Speed Diesel and Kerosene oil and adulterants were found at the premises of the firm.

He has submitted that as per the test reports dated 20.05.2010 of the Quality Control Laboratory of BPCL, the samples of the petroleum products collected from the premises did not conform to the standard specifications.

He has argued that since the said laboratory is approved by Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas and is also accredited by National Accreditation Board for testing and Calibration Laboratories, the doubt expressed by the CBI v. Praveen Garg & Anr. Page No. 10 of 26 Ld. Trial Court on the correctness of the test reports by observing that the samples ought to have been sent to some other independent laboratory was unwarranted.

Lakra Oil Trading Company, was the authorized dealer of BPCL and in view of the terms and conditions of the Dealership Agreement dated 25.01.1990, she could not have transferred the dealership or the kerosene license to any other person including the respondents.

He has submitted that the prime document on which the prosecution had relied to show the involvement of the respondents was the General Power of Attorney dated 01.08.2006 alleged to have been executed by Smt. Sushila Rani in favour of the respondent no.2 but neither the original General Power of Attorney dated 01.08.2006 was produced on record nor its due execution had been proved by the prosecution.

He has submitted that since the prosecution had failed to lead any reliable evidence to prove that the business of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company had been taken over by the respondents, the Ld. He has argued that since the CBI has failed to point out any perversity or illegality in the impugned judgment, the appeal deserves to be dismissed.

ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION:
10.

On 11.01.2013, the Ld. Trial Court had framed the following CBI v. Praveen Garg & Anr. Page No. 13 of 26 charge against the respondents and Smt. Sushila Rani:
"That on or before 12.05.2010, at premises of M/s Lakra Oil Trading Company at site no.1, Block-8, Geeta Colony, Delhi, you all accused entered into a criminal conspiracy for adulteration, storage and unauthorized sale of petroleum products in contravention to dealership agreement in favour of M/s Lakra Trading Oil Company and committed malpractice within the meaning of Motor Spirit and High Speed Diesel Regulation of Supply (Distribution and Prevention of Malpractice) Order 2005 and violated the provisions of said order as well as Section 3 r/w Section 4 of Kerosene (Restriction of Use and Fixation of Ceiling Price) Order 1993 and Delhi Kerosene Oil (Export & Price) Control Order 1962 and thereby committed an offence punishable under Section 3 and 7 of Essential Commodities Act read with Section 120B IPC and within my cognizance."

Section 3 (6) of the said Order provides that no dealer, transporter, consumer or any other person shall indulge in any manner in any one or more of the malpractices.

12. Section 3 (2) of the Kerosene (Restriction on Use and Fixation of Ceiling Price) Order, 1993 provides that no dealer appointed under the public distribution system or a transporter shall sell,
distribute or supply kerosene oil under the public distribution system to any person other than the person to whom the supplies are meant for.

Section 4 of the said Order is not applicable to the facts of the present case but for ready reference, the same has been reproduced as under:
"4. Procurement, storage and sale of kerosene under the public distribution system:-
(1) No dealer having stocks of kerosene supplied under the public distribution system at the business premises, including the place of storage:-
(a) shall unless otherwise directed by the Government or CBI v. Praveen Garg & Anr.
Page No. 15 of 26 Government Oil Company, refuse to sell, distribute or supply the kerosene to any consumer on any working day, during working hours,
(b) shall keep his business premises, including the place of storage closed during working hours on any working day without the prior written permission of the Government or the Government Oil Company,
(c) shall sell, distribute or supply kerosene at a price higher than that fixed by the Government or Government Oil Company.

(2) Every dealer appointed under the public distribution system shall take all reasonable steps to ensure that adequate stocks of kerosene are available at the business premises including the place of storage at all times.

Explanation-for the purpose of sub-clauses (1) (1) the expression "working hours" means the working hour fixed by the concerned Oil Company in accordance with the Shops and Establishments Act in force in the respective State or Union Territory."

From the material available on record, it emerges that Smt. Sushila Rani was the proprietor of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company and vide Dealership Agreement dated 25.01.1990 (Ex. PW10/B),
she had been appointed as the dealer of BPCL in respect of Light Diesel Oil and Supreme Kerosene Oil.

She was also having license no. 3614/19 dated 20.02.1990 (Ex. PW5/2), which had been renewed till 19.02.2011, issued by the Food and Supply Department, Govt. of NCT of Delhi for procuring and supply of kerosene oil under public distribution system.

Further, the premises i.e.
Site No.1, Geeta Colony, Block-8, Delhi had also been allotted to her for storage and running the distributorship of BPCL vide DDA Allotment No. F7(20)/87/MP/DDA dated 12.02.1988 (Ex.
PW10/A).

15. The case of the prosecution is that in or around the year 2006, the respondent no.1 Sh. Praveen Garg took over the business of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company from its proprietor Smt. Sushila Rani and got executed a General Power of Attorney dated 01.08.2006 from her in favour of the respondent no.2 Sh. Mukesh Goel authorizing him to manage the affairs of the said firm and that in lieu thereof, the respondent no.1 used to pay an amount of Rs.15,000/- per month to Smt. Sushila Rani.
CBI v. Praveen Garg & Anr.
Page No. 17 of 26 16.

Attested copy of the General Power of Attorney (GPA) dated 01.08.2006, which had been seized from Smt. Sushila Rani, was produced on record along with the production cum seizure memo dated 21.10.2010 (Ex. PW16/F).

The said copy of GPA had been attested by the Vice Principal of a Govt.
school.

The Ld. Trial Court opined that the prosecution had failed to prove the said GPA by observing that neither the original GPA had been produced nor due execution thereof was proved by examining Smt. Sushila Rani, who stood discharged in view of the order of the Ld. Session Court, or by procuring any GEQD report qua her signature on the same.

17. Sr. PP for CBI has contended that the Ld. Trial Court erred in discarding the GPA and failed to appreciate that the copy thereof had been seized on its production by Smt. Sushila Rani and thus,
the execution of GPA was not in dispute.
The above contention is devoid of any merits.
Execution of the GPA was not in dispute as far as Smt. Sushila Rani was concerned.

But for reading the said document in evidence against the respondents, it was incumbent upon the prosecution to examine Smt. Sushila Rani as a witness so as to afford an opportunity to the respondents to challenge her version that the affairs of the firm had been taken over by them.

Thus, mere seizure of the CBI v.
Praveen Garg & Anr. Page No. 18 of 26 copy of GPA from Smt. Sushila Rani did not dispense with the requirement to examine her and prove the said document in accordance with law.

18. Here it is noteworthy that from the evidence led by the prosecution, it is clear that even after the execution of the alleged GPA dated 01.08.2006, Smt. Sushila Rani was looking after the day-to-day affairs of the firm.

In this regard, testimonies of the officials of BPCL i.e. PW-9 Sh. Chandra Singh Cbi vs Sh.Praveen Garg And Anr on 6 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/95741817/
8 Rawat, the then Sales Assistant, and PW-13 Sh. Deepak Trivedi, the then Deputy Manager (Sales),
are relevant.

sentences.text: They have proved the report dated 30.04.2010 in respect of the inspection of the premises of the firm as Ex. PW9/3.
The said inspection report had been signed by Smt. Sushila Rani.
Both the above witnesses had deposed that they used to inspect the premises of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company and that during the inspections, they used to interact with Smt. Sushila Rani.
The prosecution had also examined Sh. Ashok Kumar Navet, the then Food and Supply officer from the Department of Food and Supply, as PW-5.
This witness used to approve the challans submitted by the licensees to procure kerosene oil from the Oil Companies including BPCL for further distribution to the kerosene oil depots.

He proved the certified copies of the CBI v. Praveen Garg &
Anr. Page No. 19 of 26 challans issued to M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company during the period 01.01.2010 to 17.05.2010 as Ex. PW5/4 (Colly.) and stated that against the said challans, proper compliance reports of lifting and delivery of kerosene oil to the depots had been filed by the firm.
A perusal of Ex. PW5/4 (Colly.) shows that all the challans and compliance reports bear the signatures of Smt. Sushila Rani.
It is evident from the above that the business of the firm was being run by her.

Further, it is pertinent to refer to Clause 22 of the Dealership Agreement dated 25.01.1990, which provided as under:
"22.

The Dealer shall not without the consent in writing of the Company assign,
transfer or in any other manner make over this present contract or Agreement to any other person or persons whomsoever."
As per the above Clause, Smt. Sushila Rani could have assigned or transferred the dealership to the respondent no. 2 only with the written consent of BPCL and not otherwise.

It is not the case of the prosecution that any such request was received or consent in writing had been granted by BPCL.
19.
For the foregoing reasons, the case of the prosecution that Smt. Sushila Rani had transferred the business of the firm to the CBI v. Praveen Garg & Anr.
Page No. 20 of 26 respondents had remained unproved and thus, the Ld. Trial Court had rightly observed that she alone was responsible for the affairs of the firm.

20. Since Smt. Sushila Rani was the proprietor of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company and managing the affairs of the firm, the role of the respondents could have been at the most in the capacity of abettors.
21. In the backdrop of the above, the Court shall now proceed to analyze the evidence available on record against the respondents.
22. As far as the respondent no.1 Sh. Praveen Garg is concerned, admittedly, he was not present at the premises of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company at the time of surprise check on 12.05.2010.
No documentary evidence had been produced on record to show that he was in any manner associated with the said firm.

The case of the prosecution is that when the team visited the premises on 12.05.2010, three employees of the firm namely Sh. Suraj, Sh. Virendra Kumar and Sh. Giriraj met and informed that they were working for Sh. Praveen Garg.

Out of the said three employees, only Sh.
Suraj was examined by the CBI v. Praveen Garg & Anr.

sentences.text: However, in his deposition, the said witness did not depose anything against Sh. Praveen Garg.

23. Though the prosecution also examined the customers of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company to show that Sh. Praveen Garg used to deal with them on behalf of the firm but it miserably failed in the said attempt.

Out of the total number of seven customers examined, only PW-8 Sh. Sanjay Adlakha, who had worked as Manager (Accounts) with M/s. Kiran Udyog Private Limited during the years 2010 to 2012, deposed that his company used to purchase furnace oil from M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company and that Sh. Praveen Garg was running the business of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company.

He identified the signatures of Sh. Sanjay Kumar Jain, the then Director of M/s. Kiran Udyog Private Limited on the invoices vide which furnace oil was purchased and proved the same as Ex.PW8/3 (Colly.).
However, no evidence was led by the prosecution to prove as to who had signed the said invoices on behalf of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company.

Further, in his cross- examination,
PW-8 stated that he never had the opportunity to meet the person who had signed the said invoices for M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company and also expressed ignorance regarding the name of the owner of the firm.

In view thereof, his CBI v. Praveen Garg & Anr. Page No. 22 of 26 deposition that Sh.
Praveen Garg was running the business of the said firm was without any basis.

Thus, even from the oral evidence adduced by it, the prosecution had failed to show that the respondent no. 1 Sh.
Praveen Garg had any nexus with the affairs of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company.
24. Under the criminal law, conspiracy is an agreement between two or more persons to commit an illegal act or a lawful act through illegal means.
It requires involvement of at least two individuals.

In the factual matrix of the case on hand, consequent upon the discharge of Smt. Sushila Rani and in the absence of proof of any connection of the respondent no.1 Sh. Praveen Garg with M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company, the prosecution had failed to prove the charge of conspiracy.

25. Even though no separate charge in respect of the substantive offence under Sections 3 & 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 had been framed against the respondent no.2 Sh. Mukesh Goel but still this Court proceeds to delve into the material produced against him by the prosecution.

26. PW-3 Sh. Suraj, who met the surprise check team at the premises of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company on 12.05.2010, CBI v. Praveen Garg & Anr. Page No. 23 of 26 stated in his examination in chief that Sh. Mukesh Goel was the owner of the firm.

However, on being suggested in the cross examination that Smt. Sushila Rani was the owner of the firm, he resiled from his earlier deposition and stated that he did not know as to who was the owner of the firm.

In view of the same, the Ld.
Trial Court rightly observed that his testimony was of no help to the case of the prosecution.

27. Further, PW-11 Sh. Gulshan Bhudhiraja, Production Manager of M/s. Shivam Engineers and Fabricators, and PW-21 Sh. Rakesh Sharma, Partner of M/s. Steel Smith, had deposed that they had purchased Furnace Oil from M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company and that Sh. Mukesh Goel used to work for the said firm.
Here it is worthwhile to mention that as per the prosecution's own case in the charge sheet, M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company was competent to deal in Furnace Oil being the authorized dealer of BPCL.

While PW-11 exhibited three invoices of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company as Ex. PW11/B to Ex. PW11/D, PW-21 proved the invoice dated 27.09.2009 raised by M/s.
Lakra Oil Trading Company as Ex. PW21/3.

Neither of them deposed as to who had signed the said Cbi vs Sh.Praveen Garg And Anr on 6 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/95741817/

sentences.text:
The prosecution also did not lead any evidence to prove that the invoices had been signed by Sh.
CBI v. Praveen Garg & Anr.
Page No. 24 of 26 Mukesh Goel on behalf of the firm.

No doubt, it is the matter of record that Sh. Mukesh Goel had got released the tanks, generator and motor pumps of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company on superdari in the capacity of the authorized representative of the said firm.
However, merely on the said premise, it cannot be imputed that Sh. Mukesh Goel was involved in the activities for which the charge had been framed.
28. Needless to say, in order to bring home the guilt of an accused, the prosecution is required to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.

Thus, it was incumbent upon the prosecution to lead cogent and positive evidence to prove that Sh. Mukesh Goel was instrumental in unauthorized procurement and storage of High Speed Diesel at the premises of M/s. Lakra Oil Trading Company and unauthorised supply of Kerosene Oil meant for the public distribution system.

Since the prosecution failed to adduce any such evidence the substantive charge for the offence under Sections 3 & 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 would have also failed against the respondent no.2 Sh. Mukesh Goel.

CONCLUSION:
29.
In the light of above discussion, this Court is of the considered CBI v. Praveen Garg & Anr.

No illegality or perversity is found in the findings recorded in the impugned judgment dated 06.10.2023.
Resultantly, the appeal filed by the CBI is hereby dismissed.
